title: Metric prefixes and conversions
blurb: Read any metric prefix, slide between units by powers of 10, and convert doses, volumes and lengths without a decimal slip.
question: A provider orders 0.6 g of an antibiotic per day in 3 equal doses, and the capsules on the shelf contain 100 mg each. How many capsules make one dose?

teach.h: One base unit, powers of ten
teach.body: Formally, the metric system is a decimal system: each quantity has a base unit (meter for length, gram for mass, liter for volume), and a prefix multiplies that base unit by a power of 10. In plain English: learn one ladder of prefixes and it works for every unit. A kilometer is 1,000 meters, a kilogram is 1,000 grams, and a kiloliter is 1,000 liters, for exactly the same reason.

head: Prefix
Symbol
Means
Example
teach.caption: Health care uses kilo-, milli- and micro- most. Micro- sits three places below milli-, so 1 mg = 1,000 mcg.
"King Henry Died By Drinking Chocolate Milk" lists the units from largest to smallest, one power of 10 apart.

teach.h: Down the ladder, multiply. Up the ladder, divide.
teach.body: Count the steps between the two prefixes. Moving DOWN to a smaller unit, multiply by 10 for each step, so the decimal point moves right and the number gets bigger. Moving UP to a larger unit, divide by 10 for each step, so the decimal point moves left and the number gets smaller. Sense check: smaller unit, bigger number. 1 m is a short distance but it is 100 cm.

teach.h: Each step is a factor of 10
teach.caption: kilo to base is 3 steps (× 1,000). base to centi is 2 steps (× 100). base to milli is 3 steps (× 1,000).

items: 2.5 kg to g: kilo to base is 3 steps down, so × 1,000. 2.5 × 1,000 = 2,500 g. Check: 2,500 ÷ 1,000 = 2.5 kg.
450 mg to g: milli to base is 3 steps up, so ÷ 1,000. 450 ÷ 1,000 = 0.45 g. Check: 0.45 × 1,000 = 450 mg.
75 cm to m: centi to base is 2 steps up, ÷ 100. 75 ÷ 100 = 0.75 m. Check: 0.75 × 100 = 75 cm.
0.25 mg to mcg: milli to micro is × 1,000. 0.25 × 1,000 = 250 mcg. Check: 250 ÷ 1,000 = 0.25 mg.

teach.h: The jumps that appear most on the TEAS
head: Larger unit
Equals
Factor
teach.caption: Because 1 mL = 1 cm³, a box 10 cm × 10 cm × 10 cm holds 1,000 cm³ = 1,000 mL = 1 L.

teach.h: Scenario: Keisha checks a pharmacy order
teach.body: Keisha, a pharmacy technician applying to nursing school, sees an order for 0.6 g of an antibiotic per day in 3 equal doses. Capsules hold 100 mg. Step 1: 0.6 g × 1,000 = 600 mg per day. Step 2: 600 ÷ 3 = 200 mg per dose. Step 3: 200 ÷ 100 = 2 capsules per dose. Check: 2 capsules × 100 mg × 3 doses = 600 mg = 0.6 g. Answering "6 capsules" would be the daily total, not one dose.

teach.text: The two classic slips: using the wrong factor (mg to g is 1,000, not 100; cm to m is 100, not 1,000) and moving the decimal point the wrong way. Always finish with the sense check: converting to a SMALLER unit must give a BIGGER number.

items: Base units: meter (length), gram (mass), liter (volume). Prefixes are powers of 10.
Down to a smaller unit: multiply (decimal right). Up to a larger unit: divide (decimal left).
kg/g, g/mg, mg/mcg and L/mL are all 1,000. m/cm is 100. cm/mm is 10.
In multi-step problems, convert to one unit first, then answer exactly what is asked.

summary: You can now name each metric prefix, count the steps between two units and multiply or divide by the right power of 10. You can also chain conversions in dose, volume and length problems and sense-check every answer.

A.q: A lab technician records a specimen mass of 0.048 kg. What is this mass in milligrams?

whyNot.0: This applies only one factor of 1,000 (kg to g) and then labels the grams as milligrams.
whyNot.1: This converts kg to g correctly but then uses 100 mg per gram instead of 1,000: 48 × 100 = 4,800.
whyNot.3: The decimal point has moved one place too far (× 10,000,000 instead of × 1,000,000).

A.q: An IV bag holds 1.2 L. A patient receives 350 mL, and later a further 0.25 L. How many milliliters remain in the bag?
A.why: Convert to mL first: 1.2 L = 1,200 mL and 0.25 L = 250 mL. Then 1,200 - 350 - 250 = 600 mL. Check: 600 + 350 + 250 = 1,200 mL.

whyNot.0: This is the intermediate answer: 1,200 - 350 = 850 mL, before the second 0.25 L is taken away.
whyNot.1: This reads 0.25 L as 25 mL. 0.25 L is 250 mL, because 1 L = 1,000 mL.
whyNot.3: This subtracts only the 0.25 L (1,200 - 250) and leaves out the 350 mL.

A.q: Which measurement is equal to 0.07 m?
A.why: Meter to centimeter is 2 steps down, so × 100: 0.07 × 100 = 7 cm. (It is also 70 mm.)

whyNot.0: This multiplies by 10 instead of 100; there are 100 cm in 1 m.
whyNot.2: This multiplies by 1,000 (the m to mm factor) but labels the result in centimeters.
whyNot.3: This multiplies by 10,000. 0.07 m is 70 mm, not 700 mm.

B.q: A tablet contains 0.125 mg of a drug. How many micrograms of the drug does it contain?
B.why: Micrograms are smaller than milligrams, so multiply: 1 mg = 1,000 mcg, and 0.125 × 1,000 = 125 mcg. Check: 125 ÷ 1,000 = 0.125 mg.

whyNot.0: This moves the decimal point only one place (× 10).
whyNot.1: This uses a factor of 100. Milli to micro is a factor of 1,000.
whyNot.2: This divides by 1,000. Converting to the smaller unit must give a bigger number.

B.q: A charity race is 5 km long and a track lap is 400 m. How many laps of the track equal the race distance?
B.why: Same units first: 5 km × 1,000 = 5,000 m. Then 5,000 ÷ 400 = 12.5 laps. Check: 12.5 × 400 = 5,000 m.

whyNot.1: This treats 5 km as 500 m (a factor of 100 instead of 1,000).
whyNot.2: This treats 5 km as 50,000 m (a factor of 10,000).
whyNot.3: This divides the wrong way round: 400 ÷ 5,000 = 0.08.

B.q: Which calculation correctly converts 3,600 mg to grams?
B.why: Grams are larger than milligrams, so divide by the factor between them, 1,000: 3,600 ÷ 1,000 = 3.6 g.

whyNot.0: Multiplying makes the number bigger, but converting to a larger unit must make it smaller.
whyNot.1: Dividing is right, but the factor is 1,000 mg per gram, not 100.
whyNot.3: This both multiplies (wrong direction) and uses 100 (wrong factor).

C.q: Which list orders these distances from least to greatest: 0.5 km, 450 m, 52,000 cm, 480,000 mm?

whyNot.0: This divides 480,000 mm by 100 (giving 4,800 m) instead of by 1,000, so it ends up last.
whyNot.2: This orders the raw numbers and ignores the units entirely.
whyNot.3: This divides 52,000 cm by 1,000 (giving 52 m) instead of by 100, so it ends up first.

C.q: A provider orders 0.6 g of an antibiotic per day, given in 3 equal doses. Each capsule contains 100 mg. How many capsules are given per dose?
C.why: 0.6 g × 1,000 = 600 mg per day. 600 ÷ 3 = 200 mg per dose. 200 ÷ 100 = 2 capsules. Check: 2 × 100 × 3 = 600 mg.

whyNot.0: 6 capsules is the whole day's amount (600 ÷ 100); the question asks for one dose.
whyNot.1: This converts 0.6 g to 6,000 mg (× 10,000), so every later step is 10 times too big.
whyNot.2: This converts 0.6 g to 60 mg (× 100), so every later step is 10 times too small.

C.q: A rectangular container measures 25 cm by 12 cm by 8 cm. Using 1 mL = 1 cm³, how many liters does it hold when full?

whyNot.1: This divides by 100 instead of 1,000; there are 1,000 mL in a liter.
whyNot.2: This divides by 10,000, one place too far.

reteach.title: Think of money
reteach.question: Dollars, dimes and cents also go up and down in tens. How does that make metric conversion feel familiar?

blocks.body: A dollar is 10 dimes or 100 cents, so turning dollars into cents means multiplying by 100, and turning cents back into dollars means dividing by 100. Meters and centimeters work exactly the same way: 1 m = 100 cm. Grams to milligrams is like dollars to tenths of a cent: 1,000 of the small unit in every big one. Swap a big unit for small ones and you get MORE pieces.

blocks.h: Money and metric side by side
blocks.caption: The same thinking scales up: 1 kg = 1,000 g, just as $1,000 is a thousand $1 bills.

blocks.text: Nobody thinks $2 is 0.02 cents. Apply the same instinct: 2 g is 2,000 mg, never 0.002 mg.

explain.body: Kilo- means 1,000 of the base unit. Deci- means one-tenth, centi- one-hundredth, milli- one-thousandth and micro- one-millionth. So 1 L = 10 dL = 100 cL = 1,000 mL.

test.q: How many deciliters are in 3.2 L?

whyNot.0: This divides by 10; deciliters are smaller, so the number must get bigger.

explain.body: Going to a smaller unit, multiply (the decimal point moves right). Going to a larger unit, divide (the decimal point moves left). One place for each step on the ladder.

test.q: A suture is 4.5 m long. What is its length in millimeters?
test.why: m to mm is 3 steps down, × 1,000: 4.5 × 1,000 = 4,500 mm.

whyNot.0: This divides by 1,000, the wrong direction.
whyNot.1: This multiplies by 100, the m to cm factor.
whyNot.3: This multiplies by 10,000, one place too far.

explain.body: kg to g, g to mg, mg to mcg and L to mL are all factors of 1,000. Moving up any one of them, divide by 1,000: 3,420 g = 3.42 kg.

test.q: A newborn weighs 3,420 g. What is the newborn's weight in kilograms?
test.why: g to kg is a factor of 1,000, upward, so divide: 3,420 ÷ 1,000 = 3.42 kg.

whyNot.2: This divides by 10,000, one place too far.

explain.body: 1 mL is exactly 1 cm³, often written cc. So a 60 cc syringe holds 60 mL, which is 60 ÷ 1,000 = 0.06 L.

test.q: An irrigation syringe holds 60 cc. What is this volume in liters?

whyNot.3: This divides by 10,000, one place too far.
